title: "Effective sample size"

Dependent draws contain less information about many posterior summaries than the same number of independent target draws. **Effective sample size** (ESS) approximates the independent-draw count that would give comparable Monte Carlo precision for a particular quantity.

## From autocorrelation to ESS

For a stationary scalar sequence of $S$ draws,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{S}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.
$$

The denominator is the integrated autocorrelation time. Positive dependence increases it and reduces ESS; negative dependence can make ESS exceed the raw draw count for some summaries.

For a function $g(\Theta)$ with posterior standard deviation $\sigma_g$,

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ESS}}}.
$$

This is uncertainty in a numerical estimate of a posterior mean, not posterior uncertainty about a linguistic quantity.

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

The code computes a textbook positive-sequence estimate for chain one's $\mu$ draws, then obtains modern four-chain bulk and tail ESS from `posterior`.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-effective-sample-size
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
production <- posterior::subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws,
  variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)
draws <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(production))
mu_chain_one <- draws$mu[draws$.chain == 1L]
acf_values <- as.numeric(acf(mu_chain_one, lag.max = 40L,
                             plot = FALSE, demean = TRUE)$acf)[-1]
first_nonpositive <- which(acf_values <= 0)
if (length(first_nonpositive)) {
  keep <- first_nonpositive[1] - 1L
  acf_values <- if (keep > 0L) acf_values[seq_len(keep)] else numeric(0)
}
integrated_time <- 1 + 2 * sum(acf_values)
textbook_ess <- length(mu_chain_one) / integrated_time

mu_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(production, variable = "mu")
sigma_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(production, variable = "sigma")
ess_summary <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("chain-one textbook mu", "four-chain bulk mu",
               "four-chain tail mu", "four-chain bulk sigma",
               "four-chain tail sigma"),
  ess = c(
    textbook_ess,
    posterior::ess_bulk(mu_draws),
    posterior::ess_tail(mu_draws),
    posterior::ess_bulk(sigma_draws),
    posterior::ess_tail(sigma_draws)
  )
)
posterior_sd_mu <- sd(draws$mu)
mcse_mu <- posterior::mcse_mean(mu_draws)

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L, length(mu_chain_one) == 1000L,
          min(ess_summary$ess) > 100L)
ess_summary
```

The one-chain textbook value is `r round(textbook_ess)`. The modern bulk ESS for $\mu$ is `r round(posterior::ess_bulk(mu_draws))`, while its tail ESS is `r round(posterior::ess_tail(mu_draws))`. These are different estimators applied to different collections of draws, so their difference is not a disagreement.

The posterior standard deviation of $\mu$ is `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_sd_mu)`, whereas the estimated MCSE of its posterior mean is `r sprintf("%.6f", mcse_mu)`. This separation is the point of ESS.

Bulk ESS uses rank-normalized draws and is useful for location summaries. Tail ESS targets information relevant to the 5% and 95% quantiles. A chain can move adequately through the center but rarely reach a tail, so the appropriate diagnostic depends on the reported summary.

ESS counts simulation information, not passages, word positions, or readers. Running longer can increase ESS and reduce MCSE. It cannot add evidence to the passage-level Student-t model or narrow its posterior target.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does positive autocorrelation tend to reduce ESS?
2. Why can bulk and tail ESS differ?
3. Which quantity changes when the sampler runs longer: posterior spread or MCSE?
4. Why is passage-level Student-t model ESS not a linguistic sample size?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Positive autocorrelations increase the integrated autocorrelation time in the denominator of ESS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Movement can be efficient near the posterior center but slow in the tails, and the two diagnostics target different summaries of the draws. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. MCSE can decrease as the run grows; posterior spread remains a property of the fixed posterior target. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. passage-level Student-t model ESS counts information in simulated posterior draws, not Provo passages, word positions, readers, or any other linguistic unit. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
